object_entity.notes: First major Latin Christian author; active in Carthage c. 195–220. Wrote at least 31 works spanning apologetics, anti-heretical polemic, and moral discipline. Coined 'trinitas' and 'tres personae una substantia'. Defender of apostolic succession, rule of faith, incarnation, and bodily resurrection. Later attracted to Montanist rigorism c. 207; teacher of Cyprian by doctrinal influence.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Tertullian introduces the refutation of Marcion's two-God theory, defending the identity of the Creator with the God of the gospel and the authority of the Old Testament as Christian Scripture.
passage.notes: Introduces the fundamental anti-Marcionite thesis: one God, Creator and Redeemer

subject_entity.notes: Bishop of Rome c. 251–253; key figure in the Novatian controversy; excommunicated Novatian and his followers; received the support of Cyprian of Carthage.

object_entity.proposition_label: Faith is transmitted through apostolic succession
object_entity.description: The bishops who succeed the apostles are authoritative guarantors of the received tradition.

context_place.notes: Imperial capital associated with the Roman church and Paul later ministry.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Eusebius preserves a letter of Cornelius of Rome describing Novatian's ordination irregularity: three simple and rustic bishops from Italy were brought to Rome and compelled to lay hands on Novatian by a counterfeit and vain laying on of hands; Novatian seized the bishopric by craft and treachery. Cornelius also lists the Roman clergy: forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers. More than fifteen hundred widows and distressed persons are supported by the Lord's grace and kindness.
passage.notes: Cornelius on Novatian's irregular ordination; Roman church size and clerical orders c. 251
